title: Single-cell-level distributions and relationships can differentiate cell-division and growth models
abstract: Complex interactions among regulatory molecules determine the rules underlying cell growth and division in microbial cells. While the governing molecular network may not always be obvious, it is well known that correlations among certain physiological quantities measured in experiments, such as birth-size, division-size, division-time, and division-added-size, can differentiate among various cell-division models, such as Timer, Sizer, and Adder. Here we show that, apart from these correlations, which we extend for the case of stochastic single-cell growth and stochastic asymmetric partitioning, probability distributions of these quantities and statistical relationships between them can also be used to differentiate between these division models. Interestingly, we show that these quantities can not only differentiate the division models, but also distinguish among the single-cell growth paradigms, such as linear and exponential growth. We then demonstrate this differentiability among various division and growth models by comparing our analytical results with published experimental data. We further show that these results remain valid even when the growth rate of a cell is correlated with the growth rate of cells from previous generations in the lineage.
summary: This work uses single-cell measurements of bacterial growth and division (like size and time) to mathematically distinguish between competing theoretical models governing cell biology. By analyzing the full statistical relationships—including variances and correlations—the authors show that these quantitative tools can pinpoint whether a species follows an Adder, Sizer, or Timer mechanism, and whether its growth is linear or exponential.
main_problem: The study aims to differentiate between various underlying cell-division (e.g., Timer, Sizer, Adder) and single-cell growth paradigms (linear vs. exponential) in microbial cells.
main_result: Analysis of statistical relationships, particularly those involving standard deviations ($\sigma$) and correlations, can successfully distinguish between the different division models and growth types.
method: The authors derive analytical probability distributions and statistical moments (means, variances, covariances) for single-cell quantities based on assumed model parameters. These theoretical predictions are then compared against experimental data.
model_or_system: The system is bacterial cell growth and division dynamics in culture. Models include Timer, Sizer, and Adder division rules, coupled with linear or exponential single-cell growth kinetics.
key_observables: Single-cell quantities: birth-size ($s_b$), division-size ($s_d$), division-time ($	au_d$), and division-added-size ($\Delta d$). Statistical measures include means, standard deviations, and Pearson Correlation Coefficients (P.C.C.).
important_parameters: Model parameters defining the distributions of size/time additions ($\Xi(s_d)$, $\Omega(\Delta d)$), growth rate distribution ($\Lambda(\alpha)$), and partitioning fraction ($\kappa( eta)$).
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include assuming independence between certain model parameters (e.g., growth rate $\alpha$ independent of size-related quantities) and using approximations like Taylor series expansions or 'sharply spiked' distributions.
figures_summary: Figures compare experimental single-cell distributions and correlation coefficients against analytical predictions for various combinations of division/growth models, with the Adder model showing better agreement in several instances.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing that correlations are useful, then demonstrating that probability distributions alone suffice. It systematically derives theoretical relationships for means, variances, and cross-correlations ($\langle \cdot angle$ vs $\sigma^2$, etc.) for different model combinations before comparing these to experimental data.
why_interesting: While the subject is biology, the methodology relies heavily on advanced statistical mechanics tools—deriving moment equations, analyzing non-equilibrium steady states, and using probability distributions to constrain underlying physical rules. This mathematical rigor connecting microscopic processes to macroscopic statistics is relevant.
